title: New NOx engine recertification rules now in force: What shipowners need to know
description:
Under the new framework, the certification procedure can be applied to an Individual Engine or an Engine Group represented by a Parent Engine, but not to Engine Family certification.
Engine Emission Test Plan becomes central A key part of the new procedure is the Engine Emission Test Plan.
This gives operators a more defined framework for demonstrating compliance without requiring testing arrangements that may be impractical for an installed engine.
For owners planning an engine modification, the NOx certification implications should be addressed early in the retrofit process, rather than once the technical work has been completed.
Where section 7.2 applies, the Engine Emission Test Plan will need to be developed and agreed before the emissions test is scheduled.
text:
The amendments to the NOx Technical Code 2008, adopted through IMO Resolution MEPC.398(83), entered into force internationally on 1 September 2026. The Norwegian Maritime Authority (NMA) has also incorporated the requirements into its national regulatory framework.

The change addresses the practical challenge of certifying engines that are already installed onboard and subsequently modified.

Under the new framework, the certification procedure can be applied to an Individual Engine or an Engine Group represented by a Parent Engine, but not to Engine Family certification. Where a substantial modification changes the engine’s rated power and/or rated speed, its nameplate must also be replaced accordingly.

Engine Emission Test Plan becomes central

A key part of the new procedure is the Engine Emission Test Plan.

Under MEPC.398(83), the plan must be prepared by the applicant and agreed with the Administration before the test is scheduled.

IMO has provided further guidance through MEPC.1/Circ.921, Guidance on the content of the Engine Emission test plan, which sets out the information that should be addressed in the plan. This includes details of the applicant and engine, existing and requested certification, the substantial modification involved and the arrangements for carrying out the emissions test.

The circular also requires information on whether testing will take place while the vessel is underway or in port, as well as details covering exhaust-gas measurement, engine power measurement, test-cycle load points and fuel-consumption measurement. For engines using low-flashpoint or gaseous fuels, the plan should also explain how the composition of the fuel used during testing will be determined.

IMO states that where particular arrangements require additional or alternative approaches, these should be agreed in advance with the Administration. Any later revisions to an agreed test plan should also be communicated to the Administration for consideration.

What about onboard testing?

The revised procedure is designed around the practical circumstances of testing an engine that is already installed onboard.

When setting the test-cycle load points, the point corresponding to 100% load may, subject to the agreed Engine Emission Test Plan, be set at no lower than 85% of the engine’s rated power. If that level cannot be achieved, the test must be deferred until at least that power level can be reached.

MEPC.1/Circ.921 further specifies that where maximum power during the test is not expected to reach the 90–100% maximum continuous rating range, but will remain at or above 85%, the test plan should explain why the higher range cannot be achieved, state the maximum power expected and provide justification for the declared rated power.

This gives operators a more defined framework for demonstrating compliance without requiring testing arrangements that may be impractical for an installed engine.

Why does this matter for retrofit projects?

The changes are particularly relevant as shipowners consider modifications to existing machinery as part of fleet efficiency and decarbonisation projects.

According to the NMA, engines that are, for example, converted to operate on alternative fuels or otherwise upgraded can benefit from a clearer and more practical certification pathway adapted to onboard NOx measurements. The amendments are intended to ensure that modified engines continue to comply with the applicable NOx requirements following upgrades or substantial modifications.

During Norway’s consultation, the Norwegian Coastal Shipowners Association highlighted the importance of ensuring that recertification does not become a barrier to measures involving existing tonnage, including engine upgrades, hybridisation and the transition to alternative fuels.

The NMA said the amendments should contribute to a clearer and more predictable framework for engine recertification.

However, an alternative-fuel conversion should not automatically be understood as triggering the new procedure in every case. The regulatory trigger remains whether the installed engine has undergone a substantial modification, as defined under the NOx Technical Code, or is being certified to a Tier for which it was not certified when installed.

What should shipowners consider?

For owners planning an engine modification, the NOx certification implications should be addressed early in the retrofit process, rather than once the technical work has been completed.

Operators should establish whether the proposed modification falls within the new procedure and engage with the relevant Administration or Recognised Organisation. Where section 7.2 applies, the Engine Emission Test Plan will need to be developed and agreed before the emissions test is scheduled.

Particular attention should be given to the engine’s existing certification, the intended modification, requested NOx Tier, rated power and speed, test arrangements and the ability to achieve the required load points.

The new requirements therefore provide a more defined route for modifying existing engines while demonstrating continued compliance with the applicable NOx limits under MARPOL Annex VI.

title: Shipping's Fuel Transition Hinges on a Number Nobody Has Agreed On Yet - gCaptain
description:
The study models fuel adoption out to 2050 under three regulatory scenarios, built around the International Maritime Organization’s Net-Zero Framework.
Until then, shipowners are committing capital to newbuilds without knowing what carbon price they will eventually face.
Only if the penalty were to rise toward USD 700 per tonne does the economic balance tip decisively toward methanol, ammonia and ethanol.
Whichever version of the Net-Zero Framework eventually clears the IMO, the size of the carbon price looks like the single biggest lever policymakers hold.
The UK, meanwhile, extended its own emissions trading scheme to domestic shipping from 1 July 2026, adding another layer of carbon cost for operators to navigate.
text:
International shipping is being asked to decarbonize before it knows what it will burn.

By Paul Morgan (gCaptain) – Vessels capable of running on methanol, ammonia or ethanol are already entering the fleet, yet a new joint study from the Global Centre for Maritime Decarbonization and Boston Consulting Group makes an uncomfortable point plain: none of these fuels is currently cheap enough to displace conventional bunkers at scale, and the regulation meant to close that gap is still being argued over.

The study models fuel adoption out to 2050 under three regulatory scenarios, built around the International Maritime Organization’s Net-Zero Framework. That framework was approved in principle at MEPC 83 in April 2025, but its formal adoption was pushed back by a full year when member states failed to reach agreement at an extraordinary session that October, following vocal opposition from Washington. The vote has now been rescheduled for 4 December 2026, straight after the IMO’s MEPC 85 session. Until then, shipowners are committing capital to newbuilds without knowing what carbon price they will eventually face.

That price turns out to matter more than almost anything else in the model. Held at the level currently on the table, USD 380 per tonne of CO2 equivalent, the study finds conventional fuel oil paired with onboard carbon capture remains the cheapest compliant option through mid-century, and the fleet stays dominated by fossil fuels. Only if the penalty were to rise toward USD 700 per tonne does the economic balance tip decisively toward methanol, ammonia and ethanol. Whichever version of the Net-Zero Framework eventually clears the IMO, the size of the carbon price looks like the single biggest lever policymakers hold.

IMO Net-Zero Framework Holds Ground After Latest Round of Climate Talks

Regional rules cannot substitute for that global signal, at least not on their own. The EU’s emissions trading system and FuelEU Maritime Regulation together cover only around a fifth of international shipping’s energy use, since they apply solely to voyages touching European ports. Outside that pool, according to the modelling, the fleet simply carries on burning what is cheapest. Brussels appears to have registered as much: on 17 July 2026, the European Commission proposed a revision to its ETS that would reserve up to 110 million emissions allowances between 2028 and 2040 specifically to subsidise the extra cost of low- and zero-emission marine fuels, an implicit admission that regulatory pressure alone was not shifting the economics fast enough. The UK, meanwhile, extended its own emissions trading scheme to domestic shipping from 1 July 2026, adding another layer of carbon cost for operators to navigate.

Two fuels emerge from the analysis as the leading long-term candidates, and neither has a clear advantage over the other. E-ammonia is cheaper to produce than e-methanol, but that saving is largely eaten up by the cost of handling a toxic, refrigerated cargo: specialist storage, larger exclusion zones, additional crew training and more complex bunkering all add up. E-methanol is simpler to handle but needs a sustainable carbon source, and the price of that biogenic CO2 turns out to be the swing factor. The study finds that below roughly USD 150 per tonne of biogenic CO2, methanol tends to win out on cost; above it, ammonia does. For both fuels, though, the price of green hydrogen remains the dominant input, accounting for more than half of the total cost of fuel use out to 2050.

There is a live data point that hints at how quickly this could move. In March 2026, engine maker WinGD and renewable energy group Envision Energy published a study of ammonia bunkering economics on the China-to-Australia route, using a real bunker price of USD 710 per tonne sourced from Envision’s Jinzhou production facility. At that price, the two companies calculated that ammonia-fuelled bulk carriers and container ships could already undercut equivalent VLSFO-powered vessels on operating cost over the first compliance period of the IMO framework. It is one route, one supplier and one moment in a volatile market, but it suggests the cost curve the GCMD-BCG model anticipates for the 2030s may already be visible at the margins today.

IMO Urged to Give Shipping Clear Investment Signal on Net Zero Pathway

Ethanol’s prospects, by contrast, look almost entirely dependent on a single regulatory decision. First-generation, food-crop-based ethanol is currently cost-competitive and available at scale, and the study credits it with supplying close to a tenth of the fleet’s energy needs by 2050 under neutral treatment. But the EU’s FuelEU Maritime Regulation already excludes food-crop biofuels from favourable treatment, assigning them the emissions factor of the dirtiest available fossil pathway instead. If that stance were applied globally, the study finds ethanol’s contribution would collapse to near zero, with the lost volume absorbed almost entirely by conventional fuel oil rather than by other alternatives. The fuel’s future, in other words, rests less on its chemistry than on how regulators choose to classify its feedstock.

On the technical side, there is encouraging evidence that engine flexibility is real rather than theoretical. Maersk’s methanol-fuelled Laura Maersk completed a full trial on 100 per cent ethanol earlier this year, building on earlier blend tests, and confirmed the fuel could be burned without compromising engine performance. That matters for the study’s central argument about optionality: dual-fuel engines let owners hedge against an uncertain fuel market, switching between compatible new fuels and conventional bunkers as prices move. But the same flexibility cuts both ways. The study shows a persistent gap between engine capacity and actual fuel consumption, with methanol dual-fuel engines making up a tenth of the projected 2050 fleet while methanol itself supplies barely two per cent of energy consumed, because owners keep the option to burn cheaper conventional fuel instead.

That gap is arguably the report’s most important finding for anyone chartering, building or financing ships today. Ordering a dual-fuel vessel does not guarantee the new fuel gets burned. Vessels last 25 to 30 years and only around 4 per cent of the global fleet turns over annually, so the engines ordered in the next few years will still be sailing in 2050 regardless of how the regulatory picture eventually settles. The study’s advice—that fleet strategy should be built around optionality rather than commitment to a single fuel—reads less like a bet on any particular winner and more like an acknowledgment that nobody, including the modellers, yet knows which fuel that will be.

The bunkering map is expected to shift unevenly as a result. Liquid fuels such as methanol and ethanol travel relatively easily, so existing hubs like Singapore and the Amsterdam-Rotterdam-Antwerp region are likely to extend their dominance simply by importing whichever new fuel their customers need. Ammonia is a different proposition. Its toxicity and low boiling point make long-distance transport expensive, which the study argues will split future ammonia bunkering into two distinct types of port: those sitting next to cheap domestic production, and those with enough existing vessel traffic to aggregate demand and justify import infrastructure through scale alone. Which type wins in any given region will depend on decisions being taken now about where hydrogen and ammonia plants get built and which ports choose to commit to the infrastructure first.

For an industry that prizes long asset lives and long-term charters, the honest conclusion is that 2050’s fuel mix is still being decided, not by any single technology breakthrough, but by a carbon price that has yet to be agreed, a biogenic CO2 market that barely exists yet, and a series of regulatory classifications still working their way through Brussels and London. The vessels ordered over the next few years will have to live with whatever answer eventually emerges.

text:
The World Shipping Council (WSC) has called on governments to close a gap in international dangerous goods regulations that allows containers carrying thousands of lithium batteries to be transported without informing carriers about the hazard.

The organisation has raised the matter amid increasing global battery transport and persistent cargo fire risk at sea.

International Energy Agency data shows that global lithium-ion battery deployment in 2025 was six times higher than in 2020 and battery demand is expected to double by 2030. Insurer Allianz has estimated that a fire occurs aboard a container ship approximately every 17 days.

At the centre of the concern is Special Provision 188 of the International Maritime Dangerous Goods (IMDG) Code.

The provision exempts small lithium batteries from certain dangerous-goods requirements when they meet specified testing, packaging and capacity criteria. However, it does not limit the number of exempt batteries that may be consolidated in a single container.

According to the WSC, a container carrying around 4 200 laptops could contain approximately 416 kilowatt-hours of stored energy – equivalent to the battery capacity of three or four electric vehicles – without requiring dangerous goods documentation or container placarding.

“A container can be packed with thousands of lithium batteries and still travel without a dangerous goods declaration,” said WSC President and CEO Joe Kramek.

“The SP188 exemption intends to simplify the transport of individual devices with small batteries, not to make entire container loads invisible.”

The WSC said lithium batteries are transported safely every day when they are properly declared and the associated risks are managed.

However, when carriers are not informed of the cargo, they cannot properly assess the risk, select an appropriate stowage position, separate the container from other cargo or prepare an informed emergency response.

“We know what can happen when hazards are invisible,” Kramek said.

“Batteries shipped under the exemption have caused serious container fires, putting people, ports, ships and the marine environment at risk.”

The WSC, supported by five governments and a coalition of industry organisations, has submitted a paper to the International Maritime Organization (IMO) outlining a potential container-level threshold.

Battery shipments exceeding the threshold will have to be declared and could also be subject to placarding requirements.

“The current rules are not working as intended,” Kramek said.

“As battery shipments continue to grow, we need a better solution that makes these cargoes visible and allows the risks to be properly managed.”

The IMO’s Sub-Committee on Carriage of Cargoes and Containers is considering the issue at a meeting in London.

The WSC has urged the sub-committee to address the matter as a priority so that improved regulations can be incorporated into Amendment 44-28 of the IMDG Code scheduled to become mandatory on January 1, 2030.

title: Are UK and Cyprus Ministers in synch over decarbonisation? - Seatrade Maritime News
description:
Speaking at Tuesday’s Capital Link Conference both Ministers agreed that providing the right regulatory framework for industry to innovate is the process by which maritime decarbonisation can be delivered.
The discussion offered a fleeting look at the strings being pulled to guide governments in their decarbonisation discussions.
Britain’s junior minister focused on autonomy and nuclear power, going as far as name checking a company, Ocean Infinity and a technology, maritime nuclear power.
“The UK is clear that in order to decarbonise, we need to be exploring a range of decarbonisation measures in shipping, especially in regards to future fuels.
The discussion at Capital Link offers a brief glimpse to the complexity that liberal democracies bring to decarbonisation negotiations.
text:
Cypriot Deputy Shipping Minister, Marina Hadjimanolis, and Keir Mather, the UK’s Transport Minister agreed on stage in London, must work with the maritime industry to deliver a workable and pragmatic decarbonisation of a hard to abate sector.

Speaking at Tuesday’s Capital Link Conference both Ministers agreed that providing the right regulatory framework for industry to innovate is the process by which maritime decarbonisation can be delivered.

But there was a tension amongst the on-stage camaraderie. Though If your ears could blink, you’d miss the distinction.

The discussion offered a fleeting look at the strings being pulled to guide governments in their decarbonisation discussions.

Britain’s junior minister focused on autonomy and nuclear power, going as far as name checking a company, Ocean Infinity and a technology, maritime nuclear power.

Conversely Hadjimanolis talked about the key role of seafarers and the “pragmatic” measures needed for “a realistic [IMO Net Zero Framework] measure, we want a measure that will give stability to the shipowners.”

Hadjimanolis’ language is reminiscent of the Greek shipowners’ who argue that the pragmatic path to decarbonisation is to use the fuel that is readily available until a workable and affordable alternative is found.

For Greek shipowners that pragmatic fuel is LNG, a fossil fuel.

It so happens that Cyprus has relatively recently discovered large reserves of the gas off its southern coast. A fact that Hadjimanolis alluded to when discussing the country’s stance ahead of the Extraordinary Session of the International Maritime Organization (IMO) last year.

Unlike Cyprus, the UK’s gas reserves are largely spent, but its nuclear expertise is an industry that can offer emission free, clean, shipping at the point of use.

Asked about the lifecycle emissions and costs of uranium as a nuclear fuel the Minister told Seatrade Maritime News in a conversation: “Obviously, nuclear in shipping is an emerging technology, the UK has got a really robust rules-based system for a lot of the issues concerned with nuclear power, whether that be waste disposal, but we need to adapt and create new regulations to ensure that nuclear shipping can be something that the UK has a share of in the future.”

All concerns said Mather around nuclear as a maritime fuel need to be “robustly worked through” in discussions at the IMO and that any regulation of maritime nuclear power must be global and agreed at the UN body.

“The UK is clear that in order to decarbonise, we need to be exploring a range of decarbonisation measures in shipping, especially in regards to future fuels. We want to be part of that work, to realise the enormous opportunity that's there,” added Mather.

What is clear, and unites the two ministers, is that their comments on emissions control and clean fuels are secondary to requirement of boosting national income.

Cyprus officials argued last year that it was likely that Cyprus would vote against the NZF, in defiance of a pan-EU agreement, while in the UK the Labour government could still tarnish its green credentials by approving new drilling in the North Sea for oil and gas.

Meanwhile, Mather’s mention of Ocean Infinity was no slip of the tongue. The company is a technology company that specialises amongst other things in seabed mapping and autonomous vessels, such as the Kuwaiti Coast Guard’s Needlefish uncrewed surface vessel (USV).

“The UK also needs to not be shy and to be unashamedly competitive,” said Mather, “In terms of capturing market shares in what is definitely going to define the future of maritime innovation in decades to come, and I see that particularly being in autonomous shipping.”

Hadjimanolis, however, stressed the importance of Cyprus’ history in shipping forming part of the country’s valued identity, which can be found in its people.

Shipping as an entity is its people stressed Hadjimanolis, contradicting Mather’s pitch for uncrewed vessel developments.

Moderator Dora Mace-Kokota, a partner at Stephenson Harwood, noted Hadjimanolis’ comments, adding that a maritime nation is about its people: “It's also a nation that remembers and knows how to regulate and then how to act as a maritime nation,” she added, turning to Mather to ask if he had any more specific thoughts in terms of initiatives.

Mather, however, ignored the discussion on the workforce: “The first thing is that the government needs to show that we're putting our money where our mouth is in terms of the sort of direction that we want to encourage private sector companies to work with us to make those big bets about where the future of shipping and maritime is moving.”

UK government maritime proposals are about technological fixes, because London is focused on growth and developing industry is key to growth.

In Cyprus with its major shipping related companies being ship management, the largest ship management cluster in Europe according to the minister, the focus is more on crew and staffing levels.

The discussion at Capital Link offers a brief glimpse to the complexity that liberal democracies bring to decarbonisation negotiations.

It is not that Ministers are being dishonest, it is that they are viewing the challenges from their own side of the black hole, and from that unique viewpoint they are focusing on jobs and wealth.

From a climate scientists’ point of view the focus is emissions reduction and the most efficient means to achieve that, while industry is there to make money and those views of the abyss offer their own challenges.

To avoid the inevitable crash through the event horizon, with humanity disappearing, industry, government and scientists must find a system of growth that brings these competing views into a genuinely green solution for our climate.

title: Rødne Takes Delivery of New All-Electric Catamaran From Oma
description:
The vessel is 46 meters long, 11 meters wide and has a service speed of 19 knots.
"We are very satisfied with the cooperation with Oma and the delivery of the new boat.
Choosing a local Norwegian shipyard with Norwegian subcontractors gives us the security and predictability we depend on," says Lars Rødne, CEO of Rødne.
"This is our first delivery to Rødne, and we greatly appreciate the trust they have shown us.
The project is a good example of value creation that occurs when Norwegian shipping companies choose Norwegian shipyards and Norwegian suppliers," says Gunnar Jan Oma, CEO of Oma.
text:
The new combi-catamaran combines high efficiency, flexibility and sustainability. The vessel is 46 meters long, 11 meters wide and has a service speed of 19 knots. It has the capacity to transport both trucks, passenger cars and up to 97 passengers, while also being adapted for cargo handling.

M/S Rygerlys is designed to offer high comfort, and is equipped with a modern, all-electric propulsion system that enables emission-free operation on the entire route. The delivery is an important contribution to the development of more sustainable maritime transport and underlines the maritime industry's role in the green transition.

"We are very satisfied with the cooperation with Oma and the delivery of the new boat. Choosing a local Norwegian shipyard with Norwegian subcontractors gives us the security and predictability we depend on," says Lars Rødne, CEO of Rødne. "This is also of great importance after the takeover. Proximity to the shipyard, short distances and good accessibility give us security for safe operation and high regularity. This benefits both the company and the travelers ."

A Norwegian collaborative project

The vessel, made of recyclable and seawater-resistant aluminum, was built entirely at Oma Baatbyggeri in Stord in close collaboration with around 20 Norwegian subcontractors. Several local companies played a role in the construction process.

Teca AS in Stord was responsible for the installation of the electrical system, as well as the radio and navigation equipment. Servogear from Bømlo supplied the vessel's gear and propeller system, while Fjellstrand in Hardanger contributed to the construction of hull sections. Brunvoll from Tokke in Telemark has been responsible for the integration of the electric hybrid propulsion system and the vessel's monitoring system. In addition, a number of other, mainly Norwegian suppliers have been involved.

"This is our first delivery to Rødne, and we greatly appreciate the trust they have shown us. The project is a good example of value creation that occurs when Norwegian shipping companies choose Norwegian shipyards and Norwegian suppliers," says Gunnar Jan Oma, CEO of Oma.

Rygerlys has now arrived in Forsand. Here, a period of running-in and testing of the charging infrastructure and quays inland in the Lysefjord awaits, to ensure that the vessel meets all requirements for safety, quality and regularity before it is put into service.

text:
Freight intelligence platform VesselBot’s recent Decoding Maritime Emissions Q2 2026 report revealed that higher levels of vessel utilization aboard containerships are among the most important factors in reducing shipping emissions.

The company followed this by publishing a new case study, EU Emissions Trading System (ETS) Surcharges vs. Actual Voyage Exposure: What Shipment Execution Data Reveals.

The study applied the same voyage-level dataset used in the earlier report to a new question: whether carrier EU ETS surcharges match the actual regulatory exposure of the voyages generating them.

One of the main takeaways was that only shipment-execution data allows accurate benchmarking of ETS exposure. The study found that, for the same carrier, origin and EU destination, the actual regulatory cost can swing by an order of magnitude depending on port sequence, not distance.

On one route, a single UK port call before entering the EU—the UK is no longer a member of the 27-member bloc—cut the voyage’s actual ETS exposure to less than 1% of total emissions, while the published surcharge on that route stayed fixed.

More Than 20,000 Containership Voyages in Q2

But first, a reminder that the EU ETS is a carbon-pricing mechanism that requires shipping companies to purchase and surrender allowances for their greenhouse gas emissions.

Maritime transport has been included in the system since January 2024. For containerships, the EU ETS covers 100% of emissions from voyages between EU/EEA (European Economic Area) ports and 50% of emissions from voyages between EU/EEA and non-EU/EEA ports.

During the second quarter of 2026, more than 20,000 containership voyages fell within the scope of the EU ETS, either departing from or arriving at an EU/EEA port. Together, these voyages generated more than 11.8 million tonnes of CO₂e, of which 7.15 million tonnes, or 60%, were subject to allowance surrender.

With EU Allowances trading at around €80 per tonne at the end of the quarter, the allowances required to cover these emissions represented an estimated €572.4 million in carbon costs for Q2 alone.

Exposure on a Per-TEU Basis

For shippers, this means millions of euros in carbon costs may be incorporated into freight rates through EU ETS surcharges. It raises the question of how carriers are passing on these costs and whether the surcharges being charged actually reflect their underlying EU ETS exposure, VesselBot noted.

With the overall exposure in Q2 2026 exceeding €572 million, VesselBot asked what this translated to on a per-TEU basis.

Using a digital-twin model, it estimated that during the Q2 containership voyages within the scope of its analysis, 42.8 million TEUs were collectively carried, putting the estimated EU ETS exposure at approximately €13.40 per TEU.

“This figure should be treated as a directional benchmark rather than a shipment-level truth. Voyage-level TEU volumes do not represent unique containers: the same container can be counted on multiple legs as it moves through a carrier’s network, for example, Shanghai to Singapore, Singapore to Rotterdam, and Rotterdam to Hamburg,” VesselBot explained.

A single container therefore appears several times in the fleetwide transport-work calculation, while the shipper ultimately faces one surcharge tied to one specific origin and destination.

Isolating Voyages

Translating fleetwide exposure into a shipper-relevant benchmark therefore requires shipment-level execution data, and VesselBot got closer to this by isolating voyages whose origin-destination pairs do not overlap with one another.

For example, CMA CGM’s direct Singapore–Rotterdam, Singapore–Valencia and Singapore–Piraeus voyages provided a more accurate benchmark: an actual ETS cost of roughly €26–€31 per TEU, well below the carrier’s published surcharge of €56–€70 per TEU.

This did not mean that the difference between estimated ETS exposure and a carrier’s published surcharge represented an overcharge, VesselBot was swift to point out.

Energy-transition surcharges may also incorporate FuelEU Maritime costs and other carrier-specific commercial assumptions. It does mean, however, that the published surcharge alone cannot tell procurement teams whether its ETS component is proportionate to the regulatory exposure generated by a specific shipment.

“Instead, the comparison demonstrates the value of a route-specific ETS benchmark. It gives procurement teams a way to quantify how much of the published surcharge can be explained by the estimated EU ETS exposure generated by the underlying voyage, and to distinguish that regulatory cost from the other components bundled into the surcharge. With this benchmark, the question shifts from simply accepting the published surcharge to evaluating whether its ETS component is proportionate to how the shipment was actually executed.”

UK Port Call Changes Regulatory Treatment

Routing through a non-EU/EEA port before entering the EU changes the equation sharply. On seven observed Singapore–Felixstowe, UK–Zeebrugge voyages, VesselBot found that only 0.5% of total voyage emissions fell within the scope of the EU ETS, producing an exposure of about €5,150 per voyage—less than the surcharge collected from a single 100-TEU shipment on that route.

The pattern shows why a blanket per-TEU surcharge is a blunt instrument: The carbon cost of moving a container between two points can vary by an order of magnitude depending on routing, yet the surcharge charged to the shipper does not currently vary with it.

The question is therefore no longer simply what ETS surcharge a carrier publishes, but whether that surcharge can be benchmarked against the regulatory exposure generated by the shipment as it was actually executed.

“Answering that question requires shipment execution data that captures the vessel, routing, port sequence, emissions, utilization, and applicable ETS coverage behind each move. As carbon costs become a larger component of freight spend, this level of benchmarking will become increasingly important for organizations seeking greater control, transparency, and governance over transportation costs.”

‘Making Intelligence Operational’

Constantine Komodromos, CEO and co-founder of Greece-based VesselBot, said that more accurate emissions measurement was only the beginning.

“The real opportunity is to make that intelligence operational. Transportation is shaped by thousands of operational decisions, and the data behind those decisions has value far beyond reporting.

“Our focus is on helping organizations understand what is actually happening across their freight operations and use that understanding at both a strategic and tactical level to achieve reductions in costs and emissions.”

title: Hoekstra says unity 'imperative' as Greece breaks EU ranks on shipping | Euractiv
authors: Sarantis Michalopoulos, Robert Hodgson, Nikolaus J. Kurmayer
description:
The European Commission expects EU countries to present a united front at upcoming talks at the International Maritime Organization (IMO) on an elusive deal to slash global shipping emissions, Climate Commissioner Wopke Hoekstra said.
“Clearly the expectation is that the European family will be on the same page here,” Hoekstra said on Wednesday.
Washington, however, wants liquefied natural gas (LNG) recognised as a clean fuel, and has found European allies in Greece and Cyprus.
The official EU position, shared with China, remains to support the provisional agreement that targets net-zero emissions from global shipping by mid-century, and favours alternative clean fuels such as methanol.
“Any proposals must be agreed at EU level and be consistent with the EU’s agreed climate objectives and existing legislation,” another European Commission official commented.
text:
The European Commission expects EU countries to present a united front at upcoming talks at the International Maritime Organization (IMO) on an elusive deal to slash global shipping emissions, Climate Commissioner Wopke Hoekstra said.

A provisional agreement was torpedoed last year after US President Donald Trump threatened personal sanctions against officials who supported the ‘Net Zero Framework’, and Greece sided with Washington.

Asked by Euractiv whether the EU executive would take action against Athens if it were to break ranks again, Hoekstra only said that it was “very unfortunate that the world did not manage to unite” last year – and that it was “imperative” to does so next time around.

“Clearly the expectation is that the European family will be on the same page here,” Hoekstra said on Wednesday.

Maritime nations are due to gather in London in November for another go at reaching a compromise on how to decarbonise a sector responsible for about 3% of anthropogenic greenhouse gas emissions.

The proposed framework is based on increasingly stringent fuel standards, and would make ship operators pay an increasing price for the CO2 they emit. Washington, however, wants liquefied natural gas (LNG) recognised as a clean fuel, and has found European allies in Greece and Cyprus.

The official EU position, shared with China, remains to support the provisional agreement that targets net-zero emissions from global shipping by mid-century, and favours alternative clean fuels such as methanol.

Athens unmoved

But since the debacle last October, Greece has ratcheted up the rhetoric and teamed up with the US and allies like Saudi Arabia to work on an alternative proposal.

Athens recently reiterated its disagreement with the EU’s position on the matter, but the Dutch former finance minister declined to clarify whether the European Commission would launch an infringement procedure should Athens break ranks again.

While it was Athens that stuck its neck out first, Greece is not alone in harbouring doubts about the global deal: Cyprus, Italy and Malta – all of which side with Washington’s pro-LNG push – did not sign the final EU agreement in late August, instead expressing their reservations.

“In view of the critical negotiations ahead, I wish to express my strong concern with the relevant preparatory discussions at EU level,” Vassilis Kikilias, Greece’s shipping minister, said recently.

Further delay

A senior EU diplomat involved in the negotiations told Euractiv that talks were progressing. “But we can’t rule out them slipping into 2027,” he added.

The diplomat noted that there had been several proposals on the table, but a group led by Denmark, home to shipping giant Maersk, has dug in its heels.

“The camp calling for a realistic solution was open to these proposals, but we ran up against the unwavering position of northern European countries,” the diplomat noted.

There are also divisions within the European Commission, with its transport department, DG MOVE, pushing for a “realistic” deal while Hoekstra’s DG CLIMA insists LNG cannot be recognised as a clean fuel.

“We are heading towards a wall at 200 kilometres an hour,” a senior European Commission official told Euractiv, warning Europe would likely face fierce global opposition in the upcoming London talks if it insists upon its maximalist position.

“Any proposals must be agreed at EU level and be consistent with the EU’s agreed climate objectives and existing legislation,” another European Commission official commented.

text:
Yokogawa Electric Corporation (TOKYO: 6841) announces that it has received orders from Kawasaki Heavy Industries, Ltd. to supply integrated automation systems for a 40,000 m³ liquefied hydrogen carrier that will be the world's largest vessel of its type, and for two hydrogen-fueled vessels. The company will contribute to the realization of a sustainable society by supporting the promotion of new energy utilization through the provision of monitoring and control solutions for the hydrogen supply chain, including storage and transportation.

As the adoption of hydrogen accelerates, establishing a supply chain capable of safely transporting and storing large volumes of hydrogen is increasingly important. Liquefied hydrogen is expected to play a key role in such a supply chain, while efforts to use hydrogen as a maritime fuel are also progressing. In Japan, demonstration projects covering the entire hydrogen supply chain are underway for the commercialization of liquefied hydrogen.

Yokogawa will supply integrated automation systems for a 40,000 m³ liquefied hydrogen carrier and two hydrogen-fuelled vessels. The carrier is described as the world's largest of its type, with systems covering onboard monitoring, control and emergency shutdown. The Japan project supports safe large-scale maritime transport and development of the liquefied hydrogen supply chain.

The system that Yokogawa will supply for the liquefied hydrogen carrier provides integrated monitoring and control of onboard equipment and incorporates emergency shutdown functions. It supports the safe and efficient handling of liquefied hydrogen that is transported at extremely low temperatures, helping to ensure safe and reliable vessel operations. In addition, its advanced integrated control capabilities will help to improve equipment performance and reduce crew workload throughout the vessel's lifecycle.

Yokogawa has also received an order to supply integrated automation systems for marine hydrogen fuel systems (MHFS) that are to be installed on hydrogen-fueled vessels. An MHFS consists of liquefied hydrogen tanks and fuel supply equipment, and is a key technology for advancing maritime decarbonization.

These vessels are being built as part of a Green Innovation Fund project led by Japan's New Energy and Industrial Technology Development Organization (NEDO) and will support safe, large-scale maritime transportation, contributing to the development of the liquefied hydrogen supply chain and the transition to a sustainable society.

Koji Nakaoka, a Yokogawa Electric executive vice president & executive officer and head of the company's Energy & Sustainability Business Headquarters, commented, “Yokogawa has extensive experience with liquefied natural gas carriers, and our technology is also being applied to liquefied hydrogen carriers. Leveraging the technologies and expertise we have developed in the field of control and safety instrumentation, we will continue to provide solutions that support safe and reliable operations for our customers in the energy sector, including hydrogen.”

text:
The Liberia Maritime Authority (LiMA) has begun preparations for the ratification and implementation of the International Maritime Organization (IMO) 2010 Protocol on Hazardous and Noxious Substances (HNS), aimed at strengthening the country's preparedness and response to incidents involving hazardous substances transported by sea.

As part of the process, LiMA on Wednesday, September 16, 2026, hosted a stakeholders' engagement at its headquarters in Monrovia to raise awareness about the HNS Protocol and discuss the requirements and mechanisms needed for its effective implementation in Liberia.

The engagement brought together representatives from relevant government institutions, maritime industry operators, and other stakeholders involved in Liberia's maritime sector.

Speaking at the opening of the meeting, Deputy Commissioner for Domestic Vessel Registration and Safety at LiMA, John F. Harvey, said the engagement was necessary as Liberia moves toward ratifying and implementing the international instrument.

Harvey said it was important for stakeholders across the maritime sector to understand the objectives of the Protocol, its implications for Liberia, and the roles they will be expected to play once the instrument is implemented.

He urged participants to take the discussions seriously, noting that the Protocol is expected to come into full force in November 2027.

Meanwhile, Technical Officer at Liberia's Permanent Mission to the IMO, Tarnue Kpangbala, described the HNS Protocol as an important instrument for strengthening the protection of marine ecosystems while supporting the safety and sustainability of international maritime trade.

Kpangbala emphasized the need for collaboration among government institutions, maritime operators, industry stakeholders, and other relevant partners to ensure that Liberia is adequately prepared to meet the requirements of the Protocol.

The IMO 2010 HNS Protocol establishes an international liability and compensation framework for damage resulting from incidents involving hazardous and noxious substances transported by sea.

The framework is intended to strengthen preparedness, clarify liability, and provide compensation mechanisms for victims and affected parties in the event of incidents involving HNS cargoes.

For Liberia, the ratification and implementation process will require coordination among government agencies and maritime stakeholders to ensure that the necessary systems, procedures, and institutional arrangements are in place.

The stakeholder engagement provided an opportunity for participants to discuss Liberia's current level of preparedness and the steps required before the country can fully implement the Protocol.

Participants also examined the responsibilities of relevant institutions and industry actors, as well as the need for continued awareness and coordination throughout the ratification process.

LiMA said the engagement forms part of its broader efforts to ensure that Liberia's maritime sector is prepared to meet international maritime obligations and strengthen safety and environmental protection.

With the Protocol expected to come into full force in November 2027, authorities are expected to continue consultations and preparatory activities ahead of Liberia's ratification and eventual implementation.

title: US House moves to overturn California at-berth emissions requirements - SAFETY4SEA
description:
The resolution targets the US Environmental Protection Agency’s 2023 decision relating to California’s Ocean-Going Vessels At-Berth regulation.
The California Air Resources Board (CARB) says its 2020 At-Berth Regulation is intended to reduce emissions from ocean-going vessels while they are docked at California ports.
EPA originally granted California authorisation for the updated At-Berth Regulation in October 2023.
For shipowners and operators calling at California ports, the immediate regulatory requirements remain important while the congressional process continues.
Debate over the rule The House vote has highlighted opposing views over the costs, benefits and regulatory reach of California’s at-berth requirements.
text:
According to the official US House Clerk record, H.J. Res. 210 passed the House on 15 September by 216 votes to 211. The resolution targets the US Environmental Protection Agency’s 2023 decision relating to California’s Ocean-Going Vessels At-Berth regulation.

If enacted, the resolution would disapprove the EPA action under the Congressional Review Act. The measure would still need to complete the remaining legislative process before taking effect.

What does California require?

The California Air Resources Board (CARB) says its 2020 At-Berth Regulation is intended to reduce emissions from ocean-going vessels while they are docked at California ports.

The requirements do not mandate shore power as the only compliance option. According to CARB, regulated vessel visits must use a CARB Approved Emission Control Strategy, which can include shore power or approved emissions capture and control technologies, unless an exception or alternative compliance pathway applies.

Implementation has been phased by vessel type:

container, refrigerated cargo and cruise vessels have been subject to the emissions-control requirements since 2023;

roll-on/roll-off vessels and tankers calling at regulated terminals in Los Angeles and Long Beach were added in 2025;

tanker requirements are scheduled to extend to all regulated terminals from 1 January 2027.

CARB states that the regulation builds on California’s earlier at-berth requirements and seeks to reduce exposure to air pollution in communities located close to ports.

Why is the rule being challenged?

EPA originally granted California authorisation for the updated At-Berth Regulation in October 2023.

In July 2026, however, EPA transmitted the authorisation to Congress for review under the Congressional Review Act. EPA argued that the waiver should have previously been submitted to Congress and said the requirements could increase costs for shipping and place additional demands on port infrastructure and supply chains.

California disputes that assessment. Following the House vote, the state government defended the at-berth requirements on public-health grounds and cited state analysis estimating that the 2020 measures could reduce potential cancer risks in communities around ports and deliver significant health benefits.

For shipowners and operators calling at California ports, the immediate regulatory requirements remain important while the congressional process continues. The development nevertheless introduces uncertainty ahead of the next scheduled expansion of the rules to tanker calls in 2027.

Debate over the rule

The House vote has highlighted opposing views over the costs, benefits and regulatory reach of California’s at-berth requirements.

Campaign group Pacific Environment, which opposes the congressional resolutions, says the measures support investments already made in cleaner port infrastructure. According to Pacific Environment, California ports have invested more than $550 million in shore power and related electrification infrastructure at Los Angeles, Long Beach, Oakland and San Diego.

The group argues that overturning the waiver could put existing investments at risk and undermine efforts to reduce pollution around port communities.

Pacific Environment also maintains that Clean Air Act waivers have historically been treated as adjudicatory decisions rather than federal rules and therefore should not fall under the Congressional Review Act.

Supporters of the repeal take a different position. A coalition of organisations led by the American Energy Alliance urged Congress to approve the resolutions, arguing that California’s waiver authority should not allow the state to effectively determine national requirements affecting vessels, port operations and supply chains beyond its borders.

The coalition said the At-Berth and Commercial Harbor Craft waivers affect ports handling a significant share of US imports and argued that national regulatory policy should ultimately be determined at federal level.

The competing positions reflect a wider debate over how emissions reductions at ports should be balanced against infrastructure costs, operational requirements and the regulatory reach of individual states.

text:
As biofuel blends move from trials towards wider use onboard, shipowners and crews are getting a new practical tool to help manage the risks that can emerge when bunkering and consuming FAME-based fuels. The International Bunker Industry Association (IBIA) has issued its Shipboard Biofuel Blend Checklist for FAME-based biofuels as an annex to IMO document MEPC 85/INF.10, bringing the guidance into the IMO’s formal documentation.

Developed by IBIA’s Technical Working Group as part of the ongoing update of the IBIA/BIMCO Shipmaster’s Bunkering Manual, the checklist is designed to help vessel operators navigate the practical challenges associated with biofuel blends, particularly when a ship is using them for the first time.

From bunkering to machinery performance

The checklist covers the key stages of managing FAME-based biofuels onboard, including fuel assessment, compatibility checks, tank preparation, water management, bunkering operations, storage and machinery performance monitoring.

IBIA noted that the growing use of biofuel blends can bring different or additional operational risks, particularly for operators with limited experience handling the fuels. These risks can be mitigated through robust fuel-management practices before delivery and throughout the fuel’s use onboard.

The checklist is based on CIMAC Guideline 04|2024, Marine fuels containing FAME: A guideline for shipowners & operators, and is intended to serve as a practical reference for crews and operators.

A focus on first-time biofuel users

The guidance is particularly relevant as more vessels begin testing or adopting biofuel blends. For operators preparing for their first FAME-based biofuel bunkering, the checklist provides a structured framework for assessing the fuel, preparing tanks and managing the fuel once onboard.

However, IBIA stresses that the checklist applies specifically to FAME-based biofuels. For other bio-based products, operators should seek input from the original equipment manufacturer (OEM) and the ship’s Recognized Organization (RO) to establish whether the product is accepted and suitable for the vessel and its equipment.

The publication of the checklist as an IMO information document comes as the shipping industry continues to examine biofuels alongside other alternative fuel pathways in its efforts to reduce emissions.

text:
Responding to the publication of the UN Environment Programme report Limiting Overshoot: Navigating exceedance of 1.5°C and pathways towards return, which finds that as “global temperature rise gets set to cross 1.5°C, pushing climate risks and impacts to dangerous new heights, the world must strive to return to below 1.5°C as soon as possible and simultaneously reduce the vulnerability of societies, communities and economies to climate impacts… by acting now to get on an ‘overshoot, peak, and decline’ pathway”, Dr Sian Prior, Lead Advisor to the Clean Arctic Alliance said:

“The shipping sector and International Maritime Organization member states must seize the chance to play their part in halting the rise in global temperatures – getting to net zero emissions means ending the greenhouse gas emissions from burning fossil fuels to power ships – it’s clear the industry needs to rapidly decarbonise.”

“The UNEP Limiting Overshoot report highlights that the near-term necessary global response to quickly slow warming calls for deep emissions cuts, including to methane and other short-lived climate pollutants such as black carbon. These are urgent measures that can and must be taken rapidly to limit overshoot. Slashing shipping emissions of black carbon will have a near instantaneous impact not only on the Arctic, but on the regional and global climate by helping preserve sea ice.”

In response to the UNEP report, António Guterres, Secretary-General of the UN said, “we must make the overshoot as small and short as possible – limiting how high temperatures rise and how long they remain above 1.5°C. That demands an overshoot of ambition: Accelerating the phaseout of fossil fuels and the renewables revolution; Slashing methane pollution”.

“The Clean Arctic Alliance is calling on other Arctic countries to support Denmark in the creation of this new regulation requiring the use of cleaner maritime fuels in order to protect the Arctic”, added Prior. “It is important that the regulation is applied within the area used as the basis of the Arctic Monitoring and Assessment Programme (AMAP) by the Arctic Council – in order to maintain a level playing field across the whole Arctic since black carbon emissions can be transported hundreds to thousands of kilometres in the atmosphere and when emitted further south can still settle on to Arctic snow and ice.”

Black carbon is a short-lived climate pollutant, produced by the incomplete burning of fossil fuels, with an impact more than sixteen hundred times that of CO2 over a 20 year period. It makes up around 20% of international shipping’s climate impact. Not only does it contribute to warming while in the atmosphere, black carbon accelerates melting if deposited onto snow and ice – hence it has a disproportionate impact when released in and near to the Arctic.

The melting snow and ice exposes darker areas of land and water and these dark patches then absorb further heat from the sun and the reflective capacity of the planet’s polar ice caps is severely reduced. More heat in the polar systems – results in increased melting. This is the loss of the albedo effect.

Declines in sea ice extent and volume are leading to a burgeoning social and environmental crisis in the Arctic, while cascading changes are impacting global climate and ocean circulation. Scientists have high confidence that processes are nearing points beyond which rapid and irreversible changes on the scale of multiple human generations are possible. Scientists say it is now too late to save summer Arctic sea ice, and research has shown that “preparations need to be made for the increased extreme weather across the northern hemisphere that is likely to occur as a result.”

Black carbon also has a negative impact on human health including premature death and harmful effects on the cardiovascular system (heart, blood and blood vessels), and recent research has found black carbon particles in the body tissues of foetuses, following inhalation by pregnant mothers.

The need to reduce emissions of black carbon because of both the climate and health impacts has been long recognised. On land, considerable effort has been made to ban dirtier fuels in power stations, to install diesel particulate filters on land-based transport, and to improve the burning of dry wood – all to reduce emissions of black carbon and improve air quality. However, at sea the same efforts have not yet been made.

The report Black Carbon Emissions from Ships in the Arctic 2019 – 2024 provides a comprehensive analysis of tank-to-wake black carbon emissions from Arctic shipping using three geographic definitions: a latitudinal band north of 60oN (excluding the Baltic Sea and Gulf of Alaska), the Polar Code Arctic waters, as well as a broader ecological boundary defined by the Arctic Monitoring and Assessment Programme (AMAP). It estimates black carbon emissions for the years 2019, 2022 and 2024. The report examines the seasonal patterns of Arctic shipping routes, profiling vessel characteristics, fuel consumption by EEZ and vessel type as well as energy use. Historical estimates show how Arctic shipping activity and associated emissions have changed over time, while forecasts reveal how growth in emissions could affect the Arctic, and inform decisions on fuel choices, such as that proposed by PPR 13/6, operational practices and regulatory strategies.

LNG and Methane

Burning LNG as fuel has a direct impact on the Arctic due to the heating effect of CO2 and methane. Although LNG results in lower emissions of CO2 than oil-based fuels, methane – a powerful greenhouse gas – is leaked into the atmosphere at every stage of the production lifecycle including when used by ships. This means that in most cases LNG powered ships are worse for the climate than conventionally fueled vessels – i.e. ships using oil or distillate fuels such as marine diesel.

Although LNG is often touted as a cleaner alternative to other fossil fuels, it is far from it. LNG is mainly methane, with a warming effect 80 times more powerful than CO2 (over a 20 year period), and is one of the biggest drivers of global heating today. Methane emissions are responsible for 25% of global heating and pack a stronger short-term punch than carbon dioxide. Methane emissions from LNG-fueled ships grew by 150% between 2012 to 2018 (Fourth IMO GHG Study).

When burned, LNG releases methane and other pollutants into the atmosphere. In addition, the process of extracting, processing, and transporting LNG results in methane leakage and can have significant environmental impacts, including habitat destruction and water pollution. In some cases LNG is produced through fracking, which has a wide variety of social, environmental and health impacts, especially in North America.

Major oil-exporting states, including Russia, China and the United States, backed the delay, alongside flag states Panama and Liberia.
Analysis by University College London’s Shipping and Oceans Research group found that a majority of member states had returned to backing the Framework broadly as it stood when approved in 2025.

text:
A year after member states failed to adopt the International Maritime Organization’s Net-Zero Framework, the vote is due to return before the Marine Environment Protection Committee (MEPC) in October 2026.

If adopted, it would introduce the first global price on shipping’s greenhouse gas emissions.

Find your next emissions monitoring solution in our international directory.

What was agreed, and what stalled

The Framework comprises a Global Fuel Standard to reduce the greenhouse gas intensity of marine fuels, alongside a carbon pricing and reward mechanism.

It was approved in principle at MEPC 83 in April 2025, after roughly a decade of negotiation. Formal adoption was expected at an extraordinary session in October 2025.

That session ended instead in a vote to adjourn for 12 months, called by Saudi Arabia and passed 57 votes to 49, with 21 abstentions and eight delegations absent.

Major oil-exporting states, including Russia, China and the United States, backed the delay, alongside flag states Panama and Liberia. The EU and UK were among those voting to proceed.

The adjournment followed sustained opposition from the Trump administration, which had submitted an impact assessment to the MEPC arguing the pricing mechanism would impose a disproportionate economic burden on the industry.

The picture one year on

Since then, the picture has shifted, though not decisively. MEPC 84 was held in London from 27 April to 1 May 2026.

Analysis by University College London’s Shipping and Oceans Research group found that a majority of member states had returned to backing the Framework broadly as it stood when approved in 2025.

That reversed the narrow majority that voted to delay it the previous October. Alternative proposals put forward at the session failed to gather significant support.

The Clean Shipping Coalition, an environmental group, said the meeting closed with majority member state backing for the Framework, despite continued opposition from the United States, Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Panama and Liberia.

Who is still opposed

The United States remained the most vocal opponent heading into MEPC 84. Its IMO delegation lead told a pre-meeting briefing there was a clear and sizable bloc opposed, with no prospect of consensus.

Oil-producing states including Saudi Arabia, Russia, Algeria, Bahrain, Iraq, Kuwait and the UAE have separately argued that any framework must be consensus-based and reflect concerns they say the current draft does not address.

Why October is uncertain

Whether the shift in sentiment translates into the two-thirds majority required for formal adoption remains uncertain.

An intersessional working group has continued technical work on implementation guidelines between the April and October sessions, aimed at narrowing outstanding disagreements before member states vote.

What is at stake for fuel and compliance planning

For fuel suppliers and compliance testing providers, the practical stakes of the vote centre on certainty rather than direction of travel.

Adoption in October would set an implementation and enforcement timetable running alongside the EU’s existing Emissions Trading System coverage of shipping and the FuelEU Maritime Regulation.

title: Shipping's carbon data needs to get real - Splash247
description:
Method C, using fuel-flow meters, can provide fuel-consumption data in real time.
Direct measurement provides visibility into actual emissions and their relationship with operating conditions.
Direct measurement is particularly valuable when companies must choose among alternative fuels, engine modifications, efficiency technologies, new coatings, wind assistance and other investments.
Direct measurement should therefore be seen as complementary, not as a wholesale replacement.
The difference is that direct measurement can turn emissions data from merely a post-facto reporting output into an everyday management resource.
text:
Jan Mattsson, the chairman of Everimpact, makes his Splash debut today.

For many years, estimating emissions was sufficient for the shipping industry. Fuel consumption was recorded, standard emissions factors were applied, and the resulting figures were reported periodically. This created a common basis for regulation and comparison.

But carbon emissions now affect operating costs, vessel performance, customer relationships, investment decisions and access to finance. Estimates remain necessary for standardised accounting, but they are no longer sufficient for effective management. Shipping should complement calculation with direct, continuous measurement at the source.

From compliance data to operational intelligence

Most maritime emissions are determined from fuel consumption using prescribed emissions factors. Methods A and B generally rely on fuel-delivery records or changes in tank levels and therefore tend to provide retrospective information. Method C, using fuel-flow meters, can provide fuel-consumption data in real time. However, all three methods calculate emissions from fuel use rather than measuring what leaves the exhaust after combustion. Direct measurement provides visibility into actual emissions and their relationship with operating conditions.

Direct measurement changes the nature of the information. Sensors can continuously measure emissions at the exhaust and connect the results with operational data. Operators can then see how emissions vary with speed, load, route, weather, currents and engine settings.

The distinction is important. Estimated data is designed primarily for accounting. Measured data can support both accounting and action.

Better evidence for better decisions

Calculated emissions depend on the accuracy of fuel records, the characteristics of the fuel, the emissions factor selected and consistent reporting across vessels and crews. Each assumption may be reasonable, but the result remains an estimate.

Direct measurement observes actual emissions at source. It can reveal differences between assumed and real-world performance, as well as variations concealed by aggregated calculations. This matters increasingly as emissions carry a direct financial cost through carbon-pricing regimes.

More dependable information can also strengthen governance. Boards and senior management are expected to oversee emissions targets, transition plans and carbon-related risks. Their decisions are more credible when supported by evidence of actual operational performance.

Direct measurement need not compete with established regulatory methods. Under the EU Monitoring, Reporting and Verification framework for maritime transport, direct measurement—formally designated Method D—is one of four permitted monitoring methods, subject to an approved monitoring plan and independent verification. It can therefore meet formal reporting requirements while also providing operationally useful information about actual post-combustion emissions. Compared with Methods A and B, it can provide more timely information; compared with Method C, it provides evidence of actual exhaust emissions rather than values calculated from fuel consumption.

The designation ‘Method D’ comes from the EU regulatory framework, but the value of direct measurement is not confined to Europe or to regulatory reporting. Ships operate across global routes, and the same measurement can help operators understand how actual emissions vary with speed, load, fuel, weather, engine condition and operating practice wherever a vessel is sailing. This operational value exists whether or not a particular voyage falls within the EU MRV or EU Emissions Trading System.

There are potential financial benefits. Under the EU Emissions Trading System, shipping companies must surrender allowances for each tonne of verified emissions falling within the system’s scope. Fuel-based methods calculate emissions using assumptions about fuel combustion and the conversion of its carbon content into greenhouse gases. Where these assumptions produce a figure higher than actual post-combustion emissions, verified direct measurement could reduce the number of allowances required and therefore lower the associated carbon cost.

Turning measurement into reductions

A post-facto emissions report may support compliance, but it arrives too late to improve the voyage that produced it. Continuous direct measurement creates a shorter and more evidence-based management cycle: observe actual post-combustion performance, identify abnormal emissions or avoidable inefficiencies, adjust operations or maintenance, measure the result and apply successful interventions elsewhere.

This can help operators assess the effects of slow steaming, route optimisation, engine tuning, hull and propeller condition, fuel quality and changes in operational practice. An unexplained rise in emissions may provide early warning of deteriorating efficiency or a maintenance issue.

Direct measurement is particularly valuable when companies must choose among alternative fuels, engine modifications, efficiency technologies, new coatings, wind assistance and other investments. Models and manufacturer projections are useful, but owners also need to know how a solution performs on their own vessels, routes and operating profiles.

A measured baseline before an intervention, followed by comparable data afterwards, can answer practical questions: Did the investment produce the expected reduction? Is the improvement sustained? Under which conditions does it work best? Which vessels should receive it next? What is the actual cost per tonne avoided?

This reduces the risk of allocating capital on theoretical assumptions alone and helps direct investment towards measures that deliver verified results.

Building confidence across the value chain

Cargo owners increasingly seek reliable information about supply-chain emissions. Charterers want to compare vessel performance, while banks, insurers and investors are paying closer attention to transition risk and the credibility of climate commitments.

Measured, timely and traceable data can strengthen customer reporting and provide firmer evidence for sustainability-linked finance and performance-based commercial arrangements. Its value lies not merely in reporting a lower number, but in showing how that number was produced and which actions achieved the reduction.

The benefits grow when measurement extends across a fleet. Comparable data allows management to identify high- and low-performing vessels, understand the reasons for differences and establish realistic internal benchmarks. Lessons from one vessel can be tested and transferred to others.

Over time, companies can build an evidence base showing how vessel classes perform, which interventions work and where further reductions can be achieved most cost-effectively. This can improve maintenance, procurement, fleet planning, emissions forecasting and carbon-cost budgeting.

From estimated compliance to measured performance

The shipping industry will continue to need calculation methodologies. They provide consistency and allow companies, regulators and markets to work from an agreed framework. Direct measurement should therefore be seen as complementary, not as a wholesale replacement.

The difference is that direct measurement can turn emissions data from merely a post-facto reporting output into an everyday management resource. As carbon constraints tighten, shipping companies will be judged not only by the targets they announce, but by their ability to demonstrate improvements in actual operations.

The companies with the clearest view of their real emissions will be best placed to reduce costs, manage risk, make sound investments and accelerate the maritime transition.

President Cyril Ramaphosa has unveiled South Africa’s (SA) inaugural wave of six priority green hydrogen projects under the national green hydrogen programme, marking a transition from strategic planning to active project execution.

Delivered on behalf of Ramaphosa by Minister of Electricity and Energy Dr Kgosientsho Ramokgopa at the African Green Hydrogen Summit in Cape Town, the address detailed a targeted pipeline of renewable energy investments.

The flagship initiative in this initial wave is the Phelan Green Group Electro-Sustainable Aviation Fuel Project located at Saldanha Bay in the Western Cape, which has reached Final Investment Decision following a $100 million (R1.82 billion) equity commitment and secured off-take agreements, with construction set for the first quarter of 2027 and initial export deliveries scheduled for early 2029.

The initial wave also encompasses five additional major developments, including the Coega Green Ammonia Project in the Eastern Cape, a large-scale export-oriented initiative currently undergoing commercial and financial structuring toward final investment decision, and the Saldanha Hydrogen Direct Reduced Iron Project in the Western Cape, which is at the pre-feasibility stage to integrate green hydrogen with low-emission steel production.

The portfolio further features the Prieska Power Reserve in the Northern Cape aimed at supplying local industrial and agricultural demand, the Green e-Fuels Producers Green Methanol Corridor targeting European export markets for maritime transport, and the Green Hydrogen Solutions Project, a localized venture focused on meeting South African domestic energy requirements that has completed Front-End Engineering Design.

“Since last year’s Summit, we have moved from an undifferentiated pipeline to a managed priority portfolio,” Ramaphosa said. “This demonstrates that with partner support, public and private financing, and proper planning, African nations can move from a concept on paper to projects in development.”

text:
The US House has voted to overturn California’s stringent at-berth emissions regulations for oceangoing ships, setting up another federal clash over the state’s ability to impose tougher environmental standards than the rest of the country.

Lawmakers passed H.J. Res. 210 by 216 votes to 211, seeking to rescind the Environmental Protection Agency authorisation that allows California to enforce its 2020 At-Berth Regulation.

The rules require vessels calling at regulated California terminals to control emissions throughout their port stay, typically by switching off auxiliary diesel engines and connecting to shoreside electricity or using an approved alternative emissions-control system. Container, reefer and cruise ships have been covered since 2023, with roro vessels and tankers at Los Angeles and Long Beach added from 2025.

California regulators estimate the expanded regime will cost around $2.23bn but deliver $2.32bn in avoided adverse health impacts, while ultimately cutting pollution from regulated at-berth activity by around 90%.

Republican congressman Vince Fong, who backed the resolution, argued California’s requirements impose costs beyond the state because of the scale of cargo moving through its ports, warning against “costly shipping mandates” that he said could raise prices and disrupt supply chains.

California governor Gavin Newsom hit back directly after the vote.

“House Republicans just voted to choke port communities and harm our children with dirtier air,” Newsom wrote. “Why? To give Big Oil another handout.”

The dispute centres partly on California’s special status under the Clean Air Act, which allows it to seek federal authorisation for emissions standards stricter than national requirements.

The House has since widened its challenge. On Wednesday it voted 214-208 to overturn a separate EPA authorisation covering California’s Commercial Harbor Craft Regulations. Both measures still require Senate approval before reaching the president.

The California vote fits a wider retreat from maritime decarbonisation under the Trump administration. Washington has become the most vocal opponent of the International Maritime Organization’s proposed Net-Zero Framework, with the State, Commerce, Energy and Transportation departments jointly rejecting its global fuel standard and emissions-pricing mechanism as a “global carbon tax” and warning other governments against supporting it. The Department of Transportation has also rescinded Biden-era guidance that incorporated greenhouse-gas reductions into federal infrastructure funding decisions, while last year withdrawing $679m from 12 offshore wind-related projects, arguing the money should instead support conventional maritime infrastructure and US shipbuilding.

text:
The International Maritime Organization (IMO) on Wednesday (16 September) said the Shipboard Biofuel Blend Checklist for FAME-based biofuels has now been issued as an annex to document MEPC 85/INF.10.

The checklist was developed by the IBIA Technical Working Group as part of the ongoing update of the IBIA/BIMCO Shipmaster’s Bunkering Manual and is intended to help vessel operators navigate some of the practical considerations involved when bunkering and consuming biofuel blends, particularly when using them for the first time.

It covers a range of areas, including fuel assessment, compatibility checks, tank preparation, water management, bunkering operations, storage and machinery performance monitoring.

As the use of biofuel blends continues to grow, IMO said having clear and practical guidance for crews and operators is increasingly important.
